warmup.q: Redis is set to write every change to a log file, and to push that file all the way to the disk once a second. A script stops the Redis program the hard way (kill -9: no warning, no time to tidy up) while payments are being written. The computer itself keeps running. After Redis starts again, how many of the payments it had answered OK are missing?
options: About one second of payments: the file only reaches the disk once a second
None: Redis handed each change to the operating system before it said OK, and the operating system kept running
Every payment since Redis last saved a full copy of its data
Only the payment whose OK was on its way when Redis stopped
warmup.why: Before Redis answers, it has already handed the logged change to the kernel, the core of the operating system, with a call named write(). The kernel keeps those bytes in its own memory and writes them to the disk a little later, and the death of the Redis program can't take them back. In the lab, Redis answered OK to 8,894 additions to a counter before the kill, and the counter read 8,894 after the restart. The one second in the first option is what a crash of the whole machine can lose: a power cut, or the kernel itself failing. The last option describes a payment that never got its OK, so losing it breaks no promise.

sections.h: What a restart forgets, and three ways to keep a copy
sections.html:
Let's put numbers on the café's problem. In Rate limiting and idempotency keys, the payments program kept a note in Redis for each payment, stored under a key, a name such as idem:7f3a. Programs talk to Redis in commands: SET stores a value under a key, and GET reads it back. Expiry, eviction and memory sized such a store: 3 million keys, about 500 MB, all of it in RAM, the computer's working memory. RAM is fast, and it keeps nothing once the program that owns it stops.

Programs stop more often than you'd think. A new version gets installed, the machine reboots, or it runs short of memory and the OOM killer, the part of the operating system that kills a program to free memory, picks Redis. Either way, the new Redis process (a running copy of a program) starts with nothing. Every payment retried over the next 24 hours finds no note, looks new, and is charged again.

So memory holds the only live copy, and everything in this lesson is a second copy that trails behind it. Think of a café that keeps today's orders on a whiteboard. Wipe the board and they're gone. To protect them, you could photograph the board now and then. You could write each change in a notebook, or phone it to a second café with its own board. The figure shows Redis's three versions: a snapshot, a log and a replica.

Ask two questions of each copy: how far behind memory is it, and what does keeping it current cost? Inside Redis, one thread, a single path of work, runs the commands of every client (each program that talks to Redis), one at a time. So any work that thread does for a copy makes every client wait. When Redis dies, you lose exactly the changes that hadn't reached a copy yet. That gap is this lesson's model.

The simplest copy is the photograph: go through every key and write it all to a file. Redis calls this an RDB file (RDB for Redis database), named dump.rdb. It's a compact snapshot of all the data at one moment, and Redis loads it at startup before it answers anyone. The command that writes one is SAVE.

SAVE runs on the main thread, and that's its problem. In the lab, 1,000,000 payments used 83 MB of memory and made a 45 MB file. SAVE took 2,065 ms. Another client sent a GET 200 ms after the save began, and waited 1,761 ms for its answer. Nothing else ran in between, because the only thread that runs commands was busy writing a file. With 25 GB of data, the pause would last minutes.

So someone other than the main thread must write the copy, and the copy must still show one moment. If a helper wrote keys out one by one while clients kept changing them, payment 5 in the file might come from 10:00:00 and payment 900,000 from 10:00:02. A refund could be in the file without the payment it refunds. Next, we'll see how Redis gets both at once.

try.title: Lose the writes since the last snapshot
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab's Redis if it isn't running: docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d. Docker runs it in a container, a small separate machine on your computer. This Redis has the default settings: a snapshot now and then, and no log of changes. Open Redis's own command prompt with docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli and run the first three commands below. CONFIG GET save shows when snapshots happen, and INFO persistence reports how Redis keeps its copies.

In a second terminal (another command window), also in the labs folder, kill the Redis program the hard way and start it again: docker compose -f env/redis.yml kill -s KILL redis, then docker compose -f env/redis.yml start redis. Reconnect, and predict what GET payment:981 returns.
Write the payment again and run BGSAVE, which takes a snapshot in the background (the next section opens it up). Repeat the kill and the start. Predict the second GET before you run it.

code.html:
CONFIG GET save
SET payment:981 approved
INFO persistence
# kill -9 the server and start it from the second terminal, then reconnect
GET payment:981
SET payment:981 approved

GET payment:981

try.expect: CONFIG GET save prints 3600 1 300 100 60 10000: three rules, each a number of seconds and a number of changed keys. Redis takes a snapshot after an hour if at least 1 key changed, after 5 minutes if 100 did, and after a minute if 10,000 did. INFO persistence shows rdb_changes_since_last_save:1 (more if you wrote other keys since the last snapshot) and aof_enabled:0: no log. After the kill, the first GET prints (nil), which means no such key. Redis answered the SET with OK and then lost it, because no snapshot held it yet. BGSAVE answers Background saving started, and after the second kill GET prints "approved". docker compose -f env/redis.yml logs redis shows the restart: Done loading RDB, keys loaded: 1, keys expired: 0.

sections.h: Saving in the background: fork and copy-on-write
sections.html:
BGSAVE, short for background save, hands the work to a second process. To make one, the main thread calls fork(), a system call (a request a program makes to the kernel, the core of the operating system) that creates a copy of the calling process. The original is now the parent, and the copy is the child. Copying 25 GB of memory would take seconds, though, and Copy-on-write, mmap and the OOM killer, in the Operating systems track, showed the kernel's trick.

The kernel hands out memory in pages, blocks of 4 KB. Each process has a page table, the kernel's map from the addresses a program uses to the pages in RAM. fork() copies only the page table, so parent and child point at the same pages. Nothing more is copied until one of them changes a page. Then the kernel copies that one page and gives the copy to the writer. That's copy-on-write. In the café, it's the camera: the photo catches the board at one instant, even while the staff keep writing on it.

The child sees memory as it was at the moment of the fork, however much the parent changes it afterwards: the frozen picture Redis needs. It writes every key to a temporary file, temp-<pid>.rdb (pid is its process number), then renames that file to dump.rdb. A rename happens in one step, so a crash halfway leaves the old snapshot in place, never half of a new one. Meanwhile the parent goes on serving clients.

Two costs remain, and both fall on the parent. First, the fork runs on the main thread while the kernel copies the page table, and the table grows with the data. It takes 8 bytes per 4 KB page, so a 24 GB Redis has 24 GB / 4 KB × 8 = 48 MB of table to copy. The Redis docs list measured fork times of about 10 to 25 ms per GB on most machines today, and far more on some older ones. Redis reports the last fork's time as latest_fork_usec, in microseconds. In the lab, 83 MB forked in 6 to 31 ms.

Second, every page the parent changes during the save gets copied. In the demo below, a few hundred updates during one save made the kernel copy 3 to 5 MB, and 300,000 updates during another copied 27 MB (rdb_last_cow_size reports it). On a server that writes heavily, the worst case comes close to twice the memory. That's why maxmemory, the memory limit from Expiry, eviction and memory, must stay well below the machine's RAM.

The three save rules from the last Try it start BGSAVE for you. On a busy server the one-minute rule fires, so a crash loses about a minute of writes; on a quiet one, up to an hour. For a cache, a copy kept only to answer faster, that's fine: it refills from the original. For payment notes it isn't: a crash erases the newest notes, and those belong to the payments most likely to be retried.

Snapshots stay useful anyway. The file is compact, loads quickly (1,000,000 keys in about 1.5 seconds in the lab) and is easy to copy to another machine as a backup. To lose less than a minute, though, we need the notebook.

try.title: Snapshot with SAVE, then with BGSAVE
steps: With the Redis from the last Try it still running, run SnapshotDemo (Java) or SnapshotDemoKt (Kotlin) from the labs folder. It loads 1,000,000 payments. Then a second thread changes random payments, one after another, while the main thread takes a snapshot, first with SAVE and then with BGSAVE. At the end it deletes its keys.

video.title: Snapshots and the append-only file: what a crash loses

sections.h: A log of every change, and when it really reaches the disk
sections.html:
A snapshot loses minutes. To lose less, record each change as it happens, the way the café's clerk writes every order in a notebook. That's the append-only file (AOF). With the setting appendonly yes, Redis adds every command that changes data to the end of a log file. It writes them in RESP, the text format clients use to send commands. On restart, Redis reads the log from the top and runs every command again, which rebuilds memory.

But writing to a file isn't the same as writing to the disk. The page cache, writeback and fsync, in the Operating systems track, showed the two steps. write() copies bytes into the page cache, the kernel's copy of file data in RAM, and returns at once. The kernel sends those bytes to the disk later, within about 30 seconds on Linux. Only fsync(), another system call, makes the disk store them, and it waits until the disk has, often for milliseconds. In the café, the notebook lies on the desk, and now and then the clerk files the newest pages in a fireproof safe. The desk is the page cache; the safe is the disk after fsync().

So "a crash" means two different events. If only the Redis process dies (kill -9, the OOM killer, a bug), the kernel keeps running. It still holds the page cache, so every byte Redis passed to write() reaches the disk. If the whole machine dies (a power cut, the kernel itself failing, a cloud machine that vanishes), the page cache dies with it, and only what went through fsync() survives.

Redis works in turns, which Inside an in-memory store called its event loop. Each turn, it runs the commands that have arrived, then sends the replies, and it calls write() on the log before it sends them. The setting appendfsync decides when it calls fsync():

appendfsync when Redis fsyncs the process dies the machine dies
always before replying, once per turn nothing lost nothing lost
everysec (default) once a second, on a background thread nothing lost about the last second
no never: the kernel decides nothing lost up to about 30 seconds

The lab checks the column for a dying process: under all three settings, kill -9 lost no write that Redis had answered. always pays in speed: in the same 3-second test it managed 1,826 writes against 8,894 with everysec, because every turn waits for the disk. Writes from many clients in one turn share one fsync(), which helps when the server is busy.

Each setting protects against one kind of crash. Name the crash, then choose the setting.

The log has one more problem: it only grows. 100,000 INCR commands, each adding 1 to one counter, make 100,000 entries for one number. So once the log has doubled since the last rewrite and passed 64 MB, Redis rewrites it (BGREWRITEAOF does it by hand). A forked child writes the current data as a new base file, in the compact RDB format, while the parent adds new changes to a fresh increment file. A small file, the manifest, lists the files that make up the log. Since Redis 7.0 they share a folder, and Redis swaps the manifest in one step when the child is done.

Next, we'll keep a copy on another machine, for the day this one is gone for good.

That's why the lab's kill -9 tests lose nothing, under every fsync setting.

try.title: kill -9 a Redis that keeps a log
steps: Start a throwaway Redis with the log turned on, and a writer inside its container that adds one to a payment counter as fast as it can. redis-cli -r 1000000 repeats the command and prints every reply, so the last line of /tmp/acks.txt is the last value Redis answered.
After about 3 seconds, kill the container's Redis with SIGKILL (the signal kill -9 sends) and start it again. Before you compare the last answer with the restarted counter, predict the difference.

Look at the log's folder and its manifest, rewrite the log, and look again. The last line removes the container. To compare, run the first four lines again with --appendonly no --save "" (no log and no snapshots) in place of the two log settings, remove the container, and then once more with --appendfsync always.

code.title: in a terminal on your Mac
code.html: docker run -d --name sfz-aof -m 128m redis:8.10.3 redis-server --appendonly yes --appendfsync everysec docker exec -d sfz-aof sh -c 'redis-cli -r 1000000 INCR payments:settled > /tmp/acks.txt' sleep 3; docker kill -s KILL sfz-aof; docker start sfz-aof; sleep 1 docker exec sfz-aof sh -c 'tail -n 1 /tmp/acks.txt; redis-cli GET payments:settled' docker exec sfz-aof sh -c 'ls -l /data/appendonlydir; cat /data/appendonlydir/appendonly.aof.manifest' docker exec sfz-aof redis-cli BGREWRITEAOF; sleep 1 docker exec sfz-aof sh -c 'ls -l /data/appendonlydir; cat /data/appendonlydir/appendonly.aof.manifest' docker rm -f sfz-aof

try.expect: The last answer and the restarted counter match: 8894 and 8894 in the run for this lesson (yours depends on how fast Docker runs the loop). The folder holds appendonly.aof.1.base.rdb (89 bytes, the empty starting point), appendonly.aof.1.incr.aof (329,101 bytes, one entry per INCR) and the manifest: file appendonly.aof.1.base.rdb seq 1 type b and file appendonly.aof.1.incr.aof seq 1 type i startoffset 0. After Background append only file rewriting started, the files are appendonly.aof.2.base.rdb at 115 bytes, holding the one counter, and an empty appendonly.aof.2.incr.aof. With --appendonly no --save "", the counter came back empty after 8,893 answers. With --appendfsync always it reached only 1,826 in 3 seconds, and the restarted server held 1,827: Redis had logged and applied one more write whose reply never reached the client. Redis can hold more than you saw answered, never less.

refs.title: Persistence: how durable is the append-only file?

sections.h: A second server copies every change, and catches up after a break
sections.html:
Files on one machine die with it, and even a healthy restart that loads 25 GB from disk takes minutes. So the next copy lives on another server, like the second café that hears every order over the phone. The command replicaof primary 6379 names another machine and its port (the number that says which program a connection is for). It turns a Redis into a replica: a read-only copy that follows every change made on another Redis, the primary.

A new replica starts with a full copy. The primary forks, as for BGSAVE, and the child sends the snapshot straight over the network instead of into a file (repl-diskless-sync yes, the default since Redis 7.0). Meanwhile the primary holds on to the new writes it receives. The replica loads the snapshot, then applies those writes. From then on, the primary sends it every write in RESP, nearly the same bytes as the log. That's the replication stream.

The primary answers its own client first and sends to replicas without waiting for them, so replication is asynchronous: a replica is always a little behind. Each replica reports its position once a second. The position is an offset, a count of every byte of the stream so far (master_repl_offset in INFO replication). The primary also has a replication ID, a random 40-character name for its history of changes. Together, the ID and the offset name one exact version of the data: two servers at the same pair hold the same keys.

Links break: a short network failure, a replica restart, a machine frozen for a few seconds. A full copy after each would cost a fork and a transfer of all the data. So the primary keeps the newest part of the stream in memory, the backlog, 1 MB by default (repl-backlog-size). A replica that reconnects sends PSYNC <replication ID> <next byte it needs>. If the ID matches and that byte is still in the backlog, the primary answers +CONTINUE and sends only the missing bytes. That's a partial resync, getting back in step with only what was missed. Otherwise it answers +FULLRESYNC and starts over with a snapshot.

In the café, the backlog is a recording of the last few minutes of the call, so a dropped line can pick up where it stopped. The picture breaks here, though. A person who missed part of a call can ask what they missed in their own words. A replica needs the exact missing bytes, and if the recording doesn't reach back that far, it throws its copy away and starts again from a fresh photo.

In the lab, a replica that missed 100 writes got them in one message of 4,808 bytes. One that missed 20,000 writes, about 1.5 MB, needed byte 25,164 while the backlog began at byte 531,441, so it got a full resync. Size the backlog as the stream's rate times the longest break you want to ride out: at 2 MB a second, 60 seconds needs 120 MB.

A replica protects against a dead machine. But it's behind, so when it takes over, some writes the primary answered may never have reached it. Next, we'll measure that hole and see who promotes the replica.

try.title: Watch a replica continue, then start over
steps: From the labs folder, start a primary, a replica and three Sentinels (the watchers of the next section): docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml up -d --wait. The alias below saves typing. Read the replication state, write on the primary, read on the replica, and try a write on the replica.

Make a short break: freeze the replica with pause (Docker stops its container without ending it), cut its link from the primary with CLIENT KILL TYPE replica, write 100 payments, unfreeze it with unpause, and read the primary's log.

Make a long one: pause and CLIENT KILL again, then 20,000 payments (about 1.5 MB of stream against a 1 MB backlog), then unpause. Predict the log line first. Keep the containers running for the next Try it.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: alias ha='docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml' ha exec primary redis-cli INFO replication ha exec primary redis-cli SET payment:981 approved ha exec replica redis-cli GET payment:981 ha exec replica redis-cli SET payment:982 approved ha pause replica ha exec primary redis-cli CLIENT KILL TYPE replica ha exec primary redis-cli EVAL "for i=1,100 do redis.call('SET','payment:'..i,'approved') end return 100" 0 ha unpause replica; sleep 2 ha logs primary | grep -i resync # the long outage: pause and CLIENT KILL again, then ha exec primary redis-cli EVAL "for i=1,20000 do redis.call('SET','payment:'..i,'approved:EUR:1250:merchant-77') end return 20000" 0 ha unpause replica; sleep 8 ha logs primary | grep -i -E 'resync|backlog' ha exec primary redis-cli INFO stats | grep sync_

try.expect: Redis's reports still use the old words master and slave for primary and replica. INFO replication shows role:master, connected_slaves:1, slave0:ip=replica,port=6379,state=online,offset=433,lag=1, a 40-character master_replid and repl_backlog_size:1048576. The replica answers "approved", and its SET fails with READONLY You can't write against a read only replica. After the short break, the primary logs Partial resynchronization request from replica:6379 accepted. Sending 4808 bytes of backlog starting from offset 875. (your byte counts may differ a little). After the long one: Unable to partial resync with replica replica:6379 for lack of backlog (Replica request was: 6475)., then Full resync requested by replica replica:6379 (rdb-channel). The first Full resync line in the log is the replica's first full copy, from when it started. INFO stats ends with sync_full:2, sync_partial_ok:1 and sync_partial_err:1.

aside.title: If a replica has every change, why keep files on the primary too?
aside.html: Because the copies fail in different ways. A replica is always a little behind, and one power cut in one building can take both machines down together. There's also a trap the Redis docs warn about. Suppose the primary keeps no files and restarts by itself after a crash. It comes back empty, the replica faithfully copies the empty data, and now both copies are gone. Keep files on the primary, or make sure it never restarts on its own.

sections.h: Counting copies with WAIT, and moving the primary with Sentinel
sections.html:
Asynchronous copying leaves a hole. The primary answers OK to a payment note and dies a millisecond later, before sending it on. The replica takes over without it. The client was told OK, and the note is gone.

In 2013, Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen tests measured it by splitting five Redis 2.6 servers into two groups, cutting the network between them on purpose. Both groups had a primary taking writes, and Redis lost 1,126 of the 1,998 writes it had answered OK, 56%. That Redis lacked WAIT, the command we meet next (it arrived in 3.0), and had an older Sentinel. But in 2026 replication is still asynchronous, and a takeover can still lose answered writes.

WAIT 1 500 narrows the hole. It holds the connection until at least 1 replica has confirmed every write this connection sent before it, or until 500 ms have passed, and returns how many replicas did. Three details decide whether it helps you. It counts writes made on the same connection, so the write and the WAIT must travel together. The compare block below shows how in Jedis and Lettuce, the two main Redis libraries for Java and Kotlin. It undoes nothing: in the lab, with the replica frozen, WAIT 1 1000 returned 0 after 1.01 seconds, and the payment stayed on the primary, readable by every client. And a replica's confirmation means "in its memory", not "on its disk".

The Redis docs say it plainly: WAIT doesn't make Redis strongly consistent, which would mean every copy agrees before you get your answer. Treat 0 as "not confirmed yet" and alert or retry, never as "it didn't happen". WAITAOF 1 1 100 (Redis 7.2) goes further: it waits until the write has gone through fsync() on this server and on one replica.

Someone also has to promote the replica, telling it to become the new primary, and a person woken at 3 a.m. is slow. Sentinel does it: separate redis-sentinel programs, usually three, on three machines. Each one pings the primary, a tiny "are you there?" message. After down-after-milliseconds with no proper reply (30 seconds by default, 3 in the lab), a Sentinel marks the primary down in its own view, +sdown. Once enough agree, a number called the quorum (2 of 3 here), it's down for all of them, +odown. A majority then picks one Sentinel to run the takeover, the failover. That Sentinel promotes the best replica, points the others at it, and tells everyone the new address. In the lab, the switch came about 4 seconds after the primary froze.

So a program never writes the primary's address into its settings. It asks a Sentinel with SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name payments, and asks again when connections fail. Jedis's RedisSentinelClient and Lettuce's Sentinel addresses do that for you.

The majority rule is why you run three: if the network splits them, the side with one Sentinel can't promote anything. Clients on the old primary's side may still write to it, though, and those writes vanish when it rejoins as a replica. min-replicas-to-write 1 with min-replicas-max-lag 10 makes a primary refuse writes once no replica has confirmed anything for 10 seconds, which limits that loss. And the promoted replica keeps the old replication ID as a second ID, so the other replicas carry on with a partial resync.

Every copy in this lesson trails memory by something: minutes, a second, or a few seconds during a failover. For payments, the last line of defence belongs outside Redis, at the payment company or in the database.

try.title: Wait for a frozen replica, then fail over
steps: With env/redis-ha.yml still up, open a prompt on the primary: docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml exec primary redis-cli. Write a payment and WAIT for one replica.

In a second terminal in the labs folder, freeze the replica: docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml pause replica. At the prompt, write another payment, WAIT up to a second, and read the payment back. Predict both answers. Then unpause replica.

Now freeze the primary instead (pause primary) and follow one Sentinel's log with docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml logs -f sentinel-1. When +switch-master appears, ask a Sentinel where the primary is: docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml exec sentinel-1 redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name payments. Then unpause primary, wait half a minute, and run INFO replication on it. Finish with docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml down -v, which stops and removes the containers.

code.title: at the primary's redis-cli prompt
code.html:
SET payment:983 approved
WAIT 1 500
# pause the replica from the second terminal
SET payment:984 approved
WAIT 1 1000
GET payment:984

After you freeze the primary, the Sentinel log shows +sdown master payments primary 6379 about 3 seconds later, then +odown master payments primary 6379 #quorum 2/2 (sometimes 3/2), +vote-for-leader, +selected-slave slave replica:6379, +promoted-slave and +switch-master payments primary 6379 replica 6379, about 4 seconds after the pause in the run for this lesson. SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name payments now answers "replica" and "6379". About 20 seconds after the unpause, the Sentinel logs +convert-to-slave slave primary:6379, and the old primary's INFO replication says role:slave and master_host:replica. The new primary's INFO replication shows the old ID as master_replid2.

opening:
Picture a café's card reader at closing time. A customer taps for a coffee, the connection drops before the answer comes back, and the reader sends the payment again. For each payment, the payments program keeps a short note in Redis, a program that holds data in a computer's memory and answers very fast. The retry finds the note, and the customer pays once.

One night, the computer running Redis restarts for an update while a reader is retrying. A program's memory is wiped when it stops, and the notes go with it. The retry looks new, and the customer pays twice.

It's easy to trust data once Redis has said OK. But Redis says OK as soon as a change is in memory, and the settings that decide when it reaches a disk sound safer than they are.

The last lesson, Rate limiting and idempotency keys, built those notes. In this lesson, we'll crash Redis on purpose, count what it forgets, and add copies one at a time. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café's payment notes, wiped by one restart. Each copy we added shrank the loss: a snapshot to minutes, the log to nothing when only the program dies and about a second when the machine does, and a replica to the few seconds a failover can drop.

On the lab's Redis, or any Redis you can reach, run INFO persistence and look at aof_enabled and rdb_last_save_time. Then run INFO replication and look at connected_slaves. For each setting, ask which crash it is meant to survive.

Next, we'll split the keys across several primaries, and find out what changes when no single server holds all the data.

compare.title: Write a payment and count the replicas that have it

java.title: WaitForReplica.java (Jedis)
java.html: // one pipeline is one connection, so WAIT counts the replicas that have THIS write try (AbstractPipeline pipe = redis.pipelined()) { pipe.set("idem:7f3a", "PENDING"); Response<Long> replicas = pipe.waitReplicas("idem:7f3a", 1, 500); // WAIT 1 500 pipe.sync(); if (replicas.get() < 1) { log.warn("idem:7f3a is on the primary only; a failover now could lose it"); } }

kotlin.title: WaitForReplica.kt (Lettuce coroutines)
kotlin.html: // a Lettuce connection is one TCP connection, so WAIT sees the write just made on it val redis = connection.coroutines() redis.set("idem:7f3a", "PENDING") val replicas = redis.waitForReplication(1, 500) ?: 0 // WAIT 1 500 if (replicas < 1) { log.warn("idem:7f3a is on the primary only; a failover now could lose it") }

compare.note: Both send the SET and then the WAIT on one connection, because WAIT counts what that connection wrote. Jedis's RedisClient keeps a pool, a set of open connections that calls take turns using, and lends one to each call. So two separate calls can travel on two connections, and a WAIT on a connection that wrote nothing returns at once: in the lab it answered 1 in 5 ms while the replica was frozen. A pipeline, a batch of commands sent together, keeps both on one connection. Lettuce shares one connection among all callers, so WAIT always follows the write. But WAIT also holds that connection, so every other coroutine (a Kotlin task that can pause without holding a thread) using it waits up to 500 ms behind it. Give code that calls WAIT a connection of its own. In both languages the answer is a count, and your code decides what a 0 means.

worked.title: Choose how the payment notes survive crashes

steps.say: Start from what a loss costs and which failures you expect. A lost note lets one retried payment reach the payment company, the business that really moves the money, a second time. Many payment companies accept the same key and refuse a repeat, which catches it. So the target is: nothing lost when the Redis process dies, about a second when a machine dies, and a few seconds at risk during a failover. That gives the primary's settings. The # ... comments are notes for you; in a real redis.conf, the settings file, put comments on lines of their own.
steps.code:
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec            # process crash: nothing lost; machine crash: about 1 s
aof-use-rdb-preamble yes        # rewrites write a compact RDB base file
save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000    # keep snapshots too: one file to copy off the machine
maxmemory 4gb                   # on an 8 GB machine: room for copy-on-write during a fork
repl-backlog-size 256mb         # 4 MB/s of stream for about a minute of outage
min-replicas-to-write 1         # an isolated primary stops taking writes...
min-replicas-max-lag 10         # ...after 10 s without any replica's acknowledgement

steps.say: Run three Sentinels on three machines, each with the same lines. A quorum of 2 marks the primary down, and the failover itself needs a majority of the three. Five seconds of silence means a frozen or dead machine, not a short hiccup in the network.
steps.code:
sentinel monitor payments 10.0.1.10 6379 2
sentinel down-after-milliseconds payments 5000
sentinel failover-timeout payments 60000

steps.say: The program connects through the Sentinels and never names the primary. After a failover, the client asks again and follows the new primary.
steps.code: RedisSentinelClient redis = RedisSentinelClient.builder() .masterName("payments") .sentinels(Set.of(new HostAndPort("sentinel-1", 26379), new HostAndPort("sentinel-2", 26379), new HostAndPort("sentinel-3", 26379))) .build(); redis.set("idem:7f3a", "PENDING"); // goes to whichever server is primary now

alt.html: val uri = RedisURI.Builder.sentinel("sentinel-1", 26379, "payments") .withSentinel("sentinel-2", 26379) .withSentinel("sentinel-3", 26379) .build() val redis = io.lettuce.core.RedisClient.create(uri).connect().coroutines() redis.set("idem:7f3a", "PENDING") // goes to whichever server is primary now

steps.say: A few writes must survive even a machine crash: say, the record that a batch of payouts to the shops was sent to the bank. For those, wait until the write has gone through fsync() on this server and on one replica: WAITAOF 1 1 200 returns two counts. Pay the extra milliseconds only on these writes, not on every payment note. Lettuce 7.9 has no WAITAOF method, so the Kotlin version uses Jedis too.
steps.code: try (AbstractPipeline pipe = redis.pipelined()) { pipe.set("payout:batch:2291", "SUBMITTED"); Response<KeyValue<Long, Long>> synced = pipe.waitAOF("payout:batch:2291", 1, 1, 200); // WAITAOF 1 1 200 pipe.sync(); boolean safe = synced.get().getKey() >= 1 && synced.get().getValue() >= 1; // local disk, one replica's disk }

alt.html: redis.pipelined().use { pipe -> pipe.set("payout:batch:2291", "SUBMITTED") val synced = pipe.waitAOF("payout:batch:2291", 1, 1, 200) // WAITAOF 1 1 200 pipe.sync() val safe = synced.get().key >= 1 && synced.get().value >= 1 // local disk, one replica's disk }

lab.title: Measure what a crash loses, then model a replica catching up
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 17 fail: nine in ReplicationBacklogTest, a model of the backlog that needs no Docker, and eight in CrashProbeTest, which start their own Redis container and kill its Redis with kill -9. A small shell loop in that container starts Redis again on the same port, the way a real server's start-up system restarts a program that died.
In ReplicationBacklog.kt, write feed: add the length of the bytes to the offset, add the bytes to the end of the backlog, and keep only the last capacity of them.

Write psync from the comment above it, then promote. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l09.ReplicationBacklogTest' until all nine pass. Read the boundary test: why is offset 134 enough and 133 not?

In CrashProbe.java, write write, count and persistenceStat, then snapshot (BGSAVE, then wait for the child) and writeThenCrash. Run all 17 tests. The names of the three log tests are this lesson's table, written as code.
hints: The backlog's oldest byte has offset offset - backlogLength + 1. A replica at offset r needs the bytes from r + 1 on, so it can continue when r >= offset - backlogLength and r <= offset.
The missing bytes are the last offset - replicaOffset characters of the backlog: backlog.substring(backlog.length - missing).
redis.info("persistence") returns lines like rdb_bgsave_in_progress:0, separated by \r\n. Find the one that starts with field + ":".
Every CrashProbeTest test writes a fresh redis.conf and empties /data before it starts, so a failed test never leaves keys behind for the next one.

drill.title: The PSYNC decision from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write psync(replicaReplId, replicaOffset) for a primary that has replId, replId2, secondOffset, offset and a backlog string. Return CONTINUE with the missing bytes, or FULLRESYNC with the current ID and offset. Then name the two situations that force a full resync.

answer.html: PsyncReply psync(String replicaReplId, long replicaOffset) { boolean sameHistory = replicaReplId.equals(replId) || (replicaReplId.equals(replId2) && replicaOffset <= secondOffset); boolean inBacklog = replicaOffset >= offset - backlog.length() && replicaOffset <= offset; if (!sameHistory || !inBacklog) return new FullResync(replId, offset); int missing = (int) (offset - replicaOffset); return new Continue(backlog.substring(backlog.length() - missing)); } // full resync: a history the primary doesn't know (a new replica, or one that followed // another primary past the switch), or a gap the backlog no longer covers

alt.html: fun psync(replicaReplId: String, replicaOffset: Long): PsyncReply { val sameHistory = replicaReplId == replId || (replicaReplId == replId2 && replicaOffset <= secondOffset) val inBacklog = replicaOffset in (offset - backlog.length)..offset if (!sameHistory || !inBacklog) return PsyncReply.FullResync(replId, offset) val missing = (offset - replicaOffset).toInt() return PsyncReply.Continue(backlog.substring(backlog.length - missing)) } // full resync: a history the primary doesn't know (a new replica, or one that followed // another primary past the switch), or a gap the backlog no longer covers

recap: Redis keeps its data in memory, the only live copy. A snapshot, the append-only log and a replica each trail it, and a crash loses exactly the changes that hadn't reached a copy.

BGSAVE forks: copy-on-write gives the child a frozen picture while the parent keeps serving. The cost is the pause for the fork and the pages copied meanwhile, and with the default rules a crash loses minutes.

The log hands every change to the kernel with write() before Redis answers. kill -9 loses nothing under any appendfsync setting; a machine crash loses about the last second with everysec, and nothing with always.

A replica follows the stream of changes a little behind. After a break it sends PSYNC <ID> <next byte>: if the gap is still in the backlog (1 MB by default), it gets only the missing bytes, and otherwise a full copy.

WAIT counts the replicas that have this connection's writes, and undoes nothing. Sentinel (three of them: a quorum to agree, a majority to act) promotes a replica and tells programs where the primary is.
The limit: a failover can still lose a few seconds of answered writes, and one primary still holds every key in one machine's memory, with one thread running every command.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our Redis has the append-only file turned on, so payment notes can't be lost." Explain when they can still be lost, and what each risk costs to close.
explain.answer: The append-only file makes Redis log every change, and Redis hands the log to the kernel before it answers. So if only the Redis program dies, nothing it answered is lost. That part is true. But with the default appendfsync everysec, the log reaches the disk itself only once a second, so a power cut or a kernel crash loses about the last second of writes. always closes that at a large cost in speed, and WAITAOF can close it for the few writes that need it. Second, one server is one machine. If it dies for good, the log dies with it, so we need a replica. Replication is asynchronous, so when Sentinel promotes the replica, writes the old primary answered but hadn't sent yet are gone. WAIT after an important write tells us whether a replica has it, but it doesn't undo or block anything. Third, if the network splits, clients cut off with the old primary keep writing to it, and those writes are thrown away when it rejoins as a replica. min-replicas-to-write makes it refuse writes after a few seconds. So the honest statement is: we lose nothing when the program crashes, about a second when the machine dies, and a few seconds' worth on a failover or a split. For payments, we close the rest outside Redis: the payment company's own check for repeated keys, and a rule in the database (a unique constraint) that refuses a second record for the same payment.

deeper.html:
Online backups in Redis 8.10. BACKUP START makes a fresh base snapshot whether or not the log is on. BACKUP SEAL freezes the writes made since then into an increment file plus a manifest, and BACKUP LIST names the files to copy, all without pausing writes or getting in the way of the server's own log rewrites. In the lab, BACKUP LIST after the seal printed /data/backupdir/appendonly.aof.3.base.rdb, appendonly.aof.3.incr.aof and appendonly.aof.manifest. A second server started with --preload-file aof:/tmp/restore/appendonly.aof.manifest came up with every key, including one written after BACKUP START. BACKUP CLEANUP releases the files. Before 8.10, the safe way to copy the log's folder was to switch off automatic rewrites while you copied it.

A cut-off log. If the server dies in the middle of a write(), the last command in the increment file can be cut off. With the default aof-load-truncated yes, Redis drops the broken end, logs !!! Truncating the AOF at offset ..., and starts. Damage in the middle of the file is different: Redis refuses to start, and the tool redis-check-aof shows where the damage is.

When forks get slow. The Redis docs' table of fork times runs from about 9 to 13 ms per GB on physical machines, through 23 ms on one kind of virtual machine, to 239 ms per GB on older rented machines in Amazon's cloud, built on a system called Xen. On one of those, a 6.1 GB fork stopped the server for 1.46 seconds. A Linux feature called transparent huge pages makes the copying after a fork far worse. With it, memory comes in 2 MB pages, so the first write to a page copies 2 MB instead of 4 KB, and a few thousand writes can copy almost everything. The docs say to turn it off on any Redis machine.

The newer full copy. The lab's logs mention rdb-channel. Redis 8.0 changed how a full copy to a replica runs: the snapshot travels on a connection of its own while the replica keeps the live stream itself, so the primary no longer has to hold every write made during a long transfer. Valkey, a free version of Redis that split off in 2024 and is run by the Linux Foundation, a non-profit group, has a similar feature. Either way, plan for the same cost: one fork and one copy of all the data per full resync.

Reading from replicas. A replica answers reads by default even while its link to the primary is down (replica-serve-stale-data yes), so a read there can be seconds or minutes old. For the check of a payment note, read the primary.

Where this goes next. The Replication track works through the general versions of these trade-offs: followers that wait and followers that don't, failover, and what readers see while a copy lags. Its lessons on leaderless replication and on concurrent writes show what systems do when "the last failover wins" isn't good enough.
